fields.Recto: What do O, Ω and Θ each bound?
fields.Verso:
• O(f) — asymptotic upper bound: the running time grows no faster than f (worst case).
  • Ω(f) — asymptotic lower bound: no faster than f (best case, or a proven floor).
  • Θ(f) — both at once: the tight bound, "grows exactly like f".

In interviews "O(...)" is used loosely for the tight worst-case bound; a lower bound on a problem (e.g. comparison sorting is Ω(n log n)) is a different, stronger statement than a bound on one algorithm.

Source: Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §1.3 'Big-O Notation', p. 31-35

fields.Recto: The five rules that let you read a Big-O off the code without counting operations?
fields.Verso:
1. Drop constants: O(2n) = O(n). 2. Drop lower-order terms: O(n² + n) = O(n²). 3. Sequential blocks add, keeping the max: O(n) then O(n²) → O(n²). 4. Nested loops multiply: n iterations × n iterations → O(n²). 5. Recursion: write the recurrence, then solve it (or use the master theorem).

Corollary used all the time: a loop that only sometimes runs to the end is still counted at its worst case, unless you use an amortized argument.

Source: Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §1.3 'Five Common Rules', p. 36-41

fields.Recto: Amortized vs worst-case complexity — what is the difference, and the classic example?
fields.Verso:
Worst case = cost of a single operation. Amortized = total cost of m operations / m, i.e. the average per operation over a long sequence, guaranteed (not probabilistic).

Classic case: appending to a dynamic array. One append can cost O(n) (grow + copy), but growth doubles the capacity, so m appends cost O(m) in total → O(1) amortized per append. Same idea for HashMap.put (rehash is rare) and for monotonic stack loops: a while that pops is O(n) in total because each element is pushed and popped at most once.

Interview phrasing: "the inner loop is not O(n) — each element enters and leaves the stack once, so it's O(n) amortized".

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §1.5.1 (arrays/lists, amortised O(1)); Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §2.2.1, p. 17

fields.Recto: Master theorem: what does it give you, and what are the three cases?
fields.Verso:
For a divide-and-conquer recurrence T(n) = a·T(n/b) + O(n^d), compare log_b(a) with d:

  • log_b(a) > d → T(n) = O(n^(log_b a)) (leaves dominate)
  • log_b(a) = d → T(n) = O(n^d · log n) (each level costs the same)
  • log_b(a) < d → T(n) = O(n^d) (the root work dominates)

Examples: merge sort T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) → a=b=2, d=1 → O(n log n). Binary search T(n)=T(n/2)+O(1) → O(log n). Naive matrix multiply by blocks with 8 recursions → O(n³).

Source: Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §6.1.6 'The Master Theorem', p. 174-177; Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §2.2.2, p. 19

fields.Recto: Rough time budget: given n, which complexity classes are safe in a 1-2 s judge?
fields.Verso:
Rule of thumb (~10⁸ simple operations per second):

  • n ≤ 10 → O(n!), O(2ⁿ) fine
  • n ≤ 20-25 → O(2ⁿ), bitmask DP
  • n ≤ 500 → O(n³)
  • n ≤ 5 000 → O(n²)
  • n ≤ 10⁶-10⁷ → O(n log n) or O(n)
  • n up to 10¹⁸ → O(log n) or O(1) — you must not iterate over n at all

This table is why "n ≤ 20 ⇒ think exhaustive search / bitmask" and "n ≤ 10⁵ ⇒ O(n²) is dead, find the two-pointer / hash / prefix-sum trick" are reliable reflexes.

Source: Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §1.3 'Frequently Arising Running Times', p. 41

fields.Recto: What does a prefix-sum array give you, and at what cost?
fields.Verso:
pre[0] = 0, pre[i+1] = pre[i] + a[i]. Then the sum of any range is sum(l..r) = pre[r+1] - pre[l] in O(1).

Build once in O(n), answer q queries in O(q) instead of O(n·q).

Two traps: (1) it only works for invertible aggregates — sums and XOR yes, min/max no; (2) if the array is updated, each update costs O(n) to repair the prefix — that is exactly when you switch to a Fenwick tree / segment tree.

From your own solutions: Find Pivot Index (find-pivot-index), Range Sum Query - Immutable (range-sum-query-immutable), Count of Interesting Subarrays (count-of-interesting-subarrays)

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §4.2 'Sum Over a Range'; Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.2.6 (BIT motivation), p. 68

fields.Recto: How do you rewrite sum of a subarray in terms of prefix sums, and why does that unlock counting problems?
fields.Verso:
sum(i..j) = pre[j+1] - pre[i], so the condition sum(i..j) = k becomes

pre[i] = pre[j+1] - k

Instead of enumerating the O(n²) subarrays, you walk j and ask a hash map: "how many earlier prefix values equal pre[j+1] - k?" → O(n) total. This is the canonical "count subarrays with sum = k" pattern, and it generalises to (pre[j+1] - k) % m for divisible-by-m conditions.

Note when it is not needed: if all values are positive, the window sum is monotone, so a sliding window is simpler and O(1) memory.

From your own solutions: Count of Interesting Subarrays (count-of-interesting-subarrays), Count Partitions with Even Sum Difference (count-partitions-with-even-sum-difference)

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §4.2 'Sum Over a Range'; §4.7 'Windows with k Distinct Elements'

fields.Recto: What is a difference array used for?
fields.Verso:
The inverse of a prefix sum: to add v to every element of a range [l, r] in O(1), you do diff[l] += v and diff[r+1] -= v.

After all the range updates, one prefix-sum pass rebuilds the final array: a[i] = a[i-1] + diff[i].

Cost: O(1) per update, O(n) at the end. It is the right tool when you have many range additions and only read at the end (booking/interval counting, "how many events are active at time t"). If you need to read between updates, you are back to a Fenwick/segment tree.

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §4.2 'Sum Over a Range' (prefix-sum duality); Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.2.6, p. 68

fields.Recto: Hash table: what is the expected complexity of insert / lookup / delete, and what breaks that promise?
fields.Verso:
Expected O(1) for put, get, containsKey, remove — expected, not worst case.

The promise degrades when:

  • many keys collide (bad hash, or adversarial input → O(n) chains),
  • the load factor is high — Java's HashMap grows (doubles + rehashes) when the load factor exceeds 0.75, which is why puts are O(1) amortized,
  • the key's hashCode/equals is wrong or mutable after insertion.

HashMap also loses ordering: iteration order is arbitrary. If you need sorted keys or floor/ceiling, use TreeMap/TreeSet (O(log n)).

From your own solutions: Count Pairs Of Similar Strings (count-pairs-of-similar-strings)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.3.1 'Unordered Set', p. 93 and §3.3.3 'Unordered Map', p. 96; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §1.5.2 'Dictionaries'

fields.Recto: Frequency counting: when do you use an int[] instead of a HashMap?
fields.Verso:
Use an int[] bucket array when the key domain is small and bounded (characters: 26 or 128; digits: 10; values 1..n): O(1) access, no boxing, no hashing.

Use a HashMap/HashSet when keys are sparse or arbitrary (strings, big ints, coordinates).

The anagram check is the archetype: two frequency vectors are equal ⟺ the strings are anagrams. Same trick gives "at most k occurrences", "first unique character", "most frequent element", "can we permute into a palindrome" (at most one odd count).

From your own solutions: Valid Anagram (valid-anagram), Relative Sort Array (relative-sort-array)

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §2.1 'Anagrams'; Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §4.5 'Counting Sort', p. 98

fields.Recto: The 'complement' pattern: what is the standard O(n) shape for pair-sum problems?
fields.Verso:
Walk once and store what you have seen; at each element x ask for the complement (k − x):

``` for x in a: if k - x in seen: return true seen.add(x) ```

O(n) time, O(n) space, and it needs no sorting — that is its advantage over two pointers. The trade-off: two pointers on a sorted array is O(1) extra space but costs O(n log n) to sort, and it can find all pairs / handle duplicates more naturally.

Rule: unsorted + "does a pair exist" → hash; sorted (or sortable and you also need order/extremes) → two pointers.

From your own solutions: Count Pairs Whose Sum is Less than Target (count-pairs-whose-sum-is-less-than-target), Two Sum IV - Input is a BST (two-sum-iv-input-is-a-bst)

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §11.4 'The k-sum Problem'; Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.3.3, p. 96

fields.Recto: Maximum subarray sum (Kadane): the recurrence and why it is O(n)?
fields.Verso:
best_ending_here = max(x, best_ending_here + x) — either you extend the previous run or you restart at x. Track the max over the whole scan.

It is O(n) because each position is visited once and the state is a single number: the classic case where a 1-D DP collapses to one variable.

Warning about the "all negative" variant: initialise with the first element (or −∞), not 0, if the subarray must be non-empty.

From your own solutions: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock)

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §4.4 'Maximum Subarray Sum'; Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §7.1, p. 218-221

fields.Recto: Converging two pointers: what is the precondition, and why is the scan O(n)?
fields.Verso:
Start with i = 0, j = n-1 and move them toward each other. Precondition: the array is sorted (or the property is monotone in the indices), so that moving one pointer has a predictable effect on the quantity you measure.

O(n) because each step permanently discards one index — i only increases, j only decreases, so there are at most n-1 steps, each O(1). No index is ever revisited, which is what separates this from an O(n²) double loop.

Used for: pair sum = k (sorted), container with most water, palindrome check, reverse in place, 3-sum after fixing one element.

From your own solutions: Container With Most Water (container-with-most-water), Max Number of K-Sum Pairs (max-number-of-k-sum-pairs)

Source: Khamies, How to Solve Algorithm Problems, §5.1 'Two Pointers'; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §11.4 'The k-sum Problem'

fields.Recto: How do you prove that moving one pointer is safe in the converging two-pointer pattern?
fields.Verso:
Use an exchange/discard argument: show that the pointer you move can no longer be part of any better answer, so dropping it loses nothing.

Container With Most Water, h[i] <= h[j]: for any k between i and j, area(i,k) = (k-i)·min(h[i],h[k]) ≤ (k-i)·h[i] < (j-i)·h[i] = area(i,j). The shorter bar caps every container it can form, and every other partner is closer — so bar i is dead. That is why you must move the shorter side and never the taller one.

If you cannot produce such a proof, the greedy move is probably wrong (that is the usual failure mode: moving both pointers, or moving the taller one).

From your own solutions: Container With Most Water (container-with-most-water)

Source: Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §3.1 'Proving Correctness of Greedy Algorithms', p. 125-126

fields.Recto: Same-direction (fast/slow) pointers: what problem shape do they solve?
fields.Verso:
Both pointers move forward, the fast one explores and the slow one marks where to write:

``` write = 0 for read in range(n): if keep(a[read]): a[write] = a[read]; write += 1 ```

This is in-place compaction: remove duplicates from a sorted array, move zeroes to the end, remove an element, partition by predicate — all O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

The invariant: a[0..write) is the finished output, a[read..] is unexplored; nothing is lost because write ≤ read always.

From your own solutions: Apply Operations to an Array (apply-operations-to-an-array), Duplicate Zeros (duplicate-zeros)

Source: Khamies, How to Solve Algorithm Problems, §5.1 'Two Pointers'; Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.1 (arrays as linear structures), p. 30

fields.Recto: Fixed-size sliding window: the loop skeleton and the invariant?
fields.Verso:
Window of exactly k elements, sliding by one position:

``` sum = sum(a[0..k-1]) # build once, O(k) for right in range(k, n): sum += a[right] - a[right-k] # add entering, remove leaving best = max(best, sum) ```

O(n) total, O(1) extra state: you never re-scan the window, you only update the two deltas. Any associative aggregate works (sum, count of vowels, count of distinct with a frequency map).

Because the size is fixed, you can also use a prefix sum instead (pre[r+1]-pre[l]) — same complexity, more memory.

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §4.7 'Windows with k Distinct Elements'; §4.2 'Sum Over a Range'

fields.Recto: Variable-size sliding window: when is it valid, and what is the skeleton?
fields.Verso:
Valid when the property is monotone in the window: extending it can only make it more invalid, shrinking only less. Then:

``` left = 0 for right in range(n): add(a[right]) while not valid(window): remove(a[left]); left += 1 best = max(best, right - left + 1) ```

Two pointers, each moving forward only → O(n) total (each element enters and leaves once, amortized).

Why monotonicity matters: if valid can flip back and forth when the window grows (e.g. "sum ≤ k" with negative numbers), the loop is unsound and you must switch to prefix sums + hash.

From your own solutions: Fruit Into Baskets (fruit-into-baskets), Count Substrings That Satisfy K-Constraint I (count-substrings-that-satisfy-k-constraint-i)

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §4.7 'Windows with k Distinct Elements' (longest window with k distinct)

fields.Recto: What is the atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) trick for 'exactly k' window counting?
fields.Verso:
A window that must satisfy "exactly k" is not monotone, but "at most k" is. So:

count(exactly k) = count(atMost k) − count(atMost k−1)

Each atMost is a normal variable-size window that counts, for each right endpoint, how many left endpoints are valid (right - left + 1). Two O(n) passes instead of one exotic one.

Same idea for "exactly K distinct elements", "at most K zeros", "subarrays with at most K replacements".

From your own solutions: Count Substrings That Satisfy K-Constraint I (count-substrings-that-satisfy-k-constraint-i), Count Complete Subarrays in an Array (count-complete-subarrays-in-an-array)

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §4.7 'Windows with k Distinct Elements'

fields.Recto: Subarray vs subsequence vs substring — and what does each one imply for the algorithm?
fields.Verso:
• Substring / subarray = contiguous. There are O(n²) of them → prefix sums, sliding window, Kadane: you exploit that they are indexed by a pair of boundaries.
  • Subsequence = keep the order, drop elements anywhere. Exponential many → greedy two pointers (pattern matching), DP (LIS, LCS), or counting.
  • Subset = no order. → bitmask DP, backtracking, combinatorics.

Reading the statement carefully is worth points: "subarray" forbids the sorting-based solutions that "subsequence" allows, and vice versa.

From your own solutions: Is Subsequence (is-subsequence), Longest Square Streak in an Array (longest-square-streak-in-an-array)

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, ch. 3 'Sequences' (§3.3 LCS, §3.4 LIS) and §4 'Arrays'

fields.Recto: Why is building a string with += in a loop O(n²), and what is the fix?
fields.Verso:
Java String is immutable: every s += c allocates a new array and copies the whole prefix → 1+2+…+n = O(n²) and O(n²) garbage.

Fix: StringBuilder (amortized O(1) append, O(n) total), then toString() once. Use char[] when you need in-place index edits (reversals, in-place compression), and s.toCharArray() on entry.

Same trap: substring in a loop, and concatenating inside a recursive return (that is why the recursive Is Subsequence solution costs O(n²) in the worst case).

From your own solutions: Add Strings (add-strings)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §1 (strings in C/C++ vs higher-level strings) and §4.8 (sorting/using the library); Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §1.2

fields.Recto: The two string-alphabet reflexes: c - 'a' and a 26-slot array?
fields.Verso:
• s.charAt(i) - 'a' maps 'a'..'z' → 0..25, which is how you index a frequency array in O(1) instead of using a map.
  • int[] freq = new int[26] is the canonical anagram/signature: two strings are anagrams ⟺ Arrays.equals(freq1, freq2).
  • For "same letter pattern" (isomorphic, word pattern), the signature is the pairing of two frequency vectors, not the vectors themselves — check both directions.
  • Digits: c - '0'; uppercase: Character.toLowerCase.

Rule of thumb: if the problem says "lowercase English letters", reach for int[26] before any hash map.

From your own solutions: Count Pairs Of Similar Strings (count-pairs-of-similar-strings), First Letter to Appear Twice (first-letter-to-appear-twice)

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §2.1 'Anagrams'

fields.Recto: Palindrome checks: the two standard techniques?
fields.Verso:
1. Two pointers from both ends: compare s[i] and s[j], move inward. O(n) time, O(1) space. With one allowed mismatch (Valid Palindrome II), on a mismatch try skipping left or right — still O(n). 2. Expand around the centre: for each centre (n odd centres, n-1 even), grow while characters match → finds the longest palindromic substring in O(n²) without DP.

Recognition: "palindrome" + "at most k deletions/changes" → two pointers with a budget; "longest palindromic substring" → expand around centre (or Manacher, O(n)).

From your own solutions: Smallest Palindromic Rearrangement I (smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-i), Longest Palindrome by Concatenating Two Letter Words (longest-palindrome-by-concatenating-two-letter-words)

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §2.7 'Longest Palindrome of a String — Manacher'; Khamies, How to Solve Algorithm Problems, §5.1

fields.Recto: Naive substring search is O(n·m). What are the three standard improvements, and their idea?
fields.Verso:
• KMP (prefix function π): precompute, for each prefix, the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. On a mismatch you jump to π[j-1] instead of restarting → O(n+m), never re-reads a character.
  • Rabin–Karp (rolling hash): hash the pattern, then slide a hash over the text in O(1) per position (hash = (hash - s[i]·p^i)·p + s[i+m]) → O(n+m) expected; needs a collision check.
  • Z-function: z[i] = length of the longest common prefix of s and s[i:] → same substring search, plus periodicity facts.

All three trade O(m) preprocessing for the guarantee of never backtracking in the text.

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §2.4 'Searching for Patterns', §2.5 'Knuth–Morris–Pratt', §2.6 'Rabin–Karp'; cp-algorithms.com 'Prefix function — KMP' and 'String Hashing'

fields.Recto: When is a trie the right structure for string problems?
fields.Verso:
When the queries are about prefixes, not exact keys: autocomplete, "does any word start with this prefix", longest common prefix of many words, word break / replace words.

Structure: one node per character, a children map (or Node[26]), a isWord flag. Insert and search are O(L) in the word length — independent of how many words are stored, which a hash set cannot match for prefix queries.

Cost: memory ≈ total number of characters × alphabet, which is why Node[26] is used for lowercase-only and a HashMap<Character,Node> otherwise.

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.2.7 'Trie', p. 72; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §2.3 'Spell Checking with a Lexicographic Tree'

fields.Recto: Stack vs queue: operations, complexity, and the problem shape each one fits?
fields.Verso:
• Stack (LIFO): push/pop/peek at one end, all O(1). Fits nesting and undo: balanced brackets, expression evaluation (RPN), "remove adjacent duplicates", backspace simulation, DFS, function calls (recursion).
  • Queue (FIFO): enqueue at the tail, dequeue at the head, O(1). Fits fair ordering and levels: BFS, level-order traversal, scheduling (tickets, lunch queue), sliding windows.
  • Deque: both ends O(1) — the base of the monotonic queue.

Both are abstract types: ArrayDeque in Java implements both, and is the default choice over Stack/LinkedList.

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.1.1 'Stack', p. 30, §3.1.2 'Queue', p. 32; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §1.5.1-1.5.3

fields.Recto: Balanced brackets with a stack: the algorithm and the invariant it maintains?
fields.Verso:
Scan left to right: push every opener; on a closer, the stack top must be its matching opener — pop it, otherwise return false. At the end the stack must be empty.

Invariant: the stack holds exactly the openers that have not been closed yet, in order. That is why the top is always the most recent unmatched opener — LIFO matches the nesting structure of the string.

Generalises to: minimum removals to make valid, longest valid parentheses (stack of indices), and "remove k digits"-style monotonic stack problems.

From your own solutions: Valid Parentheses (valid-parentheses)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.1.1 'Stack', p. 30; Wikipedia, 'All nearest smaller values' (parenthesis matching application)

fields.Recto: Monotonic stack: definition, invariant, and why it is O(n) and not O(n²)?
fields.Verso:
A stack kept sorted (monotone) by popping everything that violates the order before pushing the new element. Each element is pushed once and popped at most once → the inner while is O(n) amortized in total.

Invariant: the stack holds the candidates that are still "alive" — the elements that could be the answer for some future position. Popping an element is the proof that it can never matter again (a nearer, better candidate exists).

Canonical use: for each position, the next greater (or smaller) element — pop while top < current, the popped element's answer is the current index. Direction of the comparison decides whether you get "next greater" or "next smaller", and scanning left→right vs right→left decides "next" vs "previous".

From your own solutions: Daily Temperatures (daily-temperatures), Final Prices With a Special Discount in a Shop (final-prices-with-a-special-discount-in-a-shop)

Source: Wikipedia, 'All nearest smaller values' (stack-based linear algorithm); Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.1.1, p. 30

fields.Recto: How does a monotonic stack solve 'largest rectangle in a histogram'?
fields.Verso:
For each bar, the largest rectangle using it as the shortest bar extends left to the previous smaller bar and right to the next smaller bar: height[i] · (right_smaller - left_smaller - 1).

A monotonic increasing stack computes both boundaries in one pass: when you pop a bar, the current index is its next-smaller, and the new top is its previous-smaller. Add sentinels (0 at both ends) to flush the stack — one pass, O(n).

This is the reference example of "stack keeps the frontier of the not-yet-dominated candidates".

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §13.3 'Largest Rectangle in a Histogram'; Wikipedia, 'All nearest smaller values'

fields.Recto: Monotonic deque: what does it buy you over a heap for 'max of every window of size k'?
fields.Verso:
A decreasing deque of indices: before pushing i, pop from the back everything ≤ a[i] (dominated), and pop from the front anything that fell out of the window (front <= i-k). Then a[deque.front] is the window maximum.

O(n) total (each index enters/leaves once) vs O(n log k) for a heap, and O(1) memory per step vs a heap of size k.

Same trick answers "minimum in all subarrays of fixed length" and the "minimum of a queue" problem, and it is what turns many O(nk) sliding-window-maximum solutions into O(n).

From your own solutions: Count Subarrays With Fixed Bounds (count-subarrays-with-fixed-bounds)

Source: cp-algorithms.com 'Minimum Stack / Minimum Queue' (finding the minimum for all subarrays of fixed length, O(n))

fields.Recto: Singly linked list: the complexity profile, and why a dummy head node?
fields.Verso:
• Access by index O(n) (no random access), insert/delete given the previous node O(1), search O(n).
  • Memory: one node allocation per element, plus a pointer — cache-unfriendly compared to an array.

Dummy (sentinel) head = an extra node before the real head. It removes every "am I deleting the first element?" special case, because the head now always has a predecessor. Same for a dummy tail in doubly linked lists. This is the single biggest source of clean linked-list code.

From your own solutions: Remove Linked List Elements (remove-linked-list-elements), Merge In Between Linked Lists (merge-in-between-linked-lists)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.1.3 'Linked List', p. 33; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §1.5.1

fields.Recto: Reverse a singly linked list in place: the three-pointer loop and its invariant?
fields.Verso:
``` prev = null; curr = head while curr != null: next = curr.next # save curr.next = prev # reverse the link prev = curr # advance curr = next return prev # new head ```

Invariant: everything before curr is already reversed, and prev is its new head. next must be saved before overwriting curr.next, otherwise the rest of the list is lost.

O(n) time, O(1) space; recursion also works but costs O(n) stack.

fields.Recto: Fast & slow pointers: three problems solved by the same trick?
fields.Verso:
Both start at head, slow moves 1, fast moves 2:

1. Middle — when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle (that is how you split for merge sort, or find the twin-sum partner). 2. k-th from the end — start fast k steps ahead, then move both until fast ends; slow is the target. (Needs a dummy when k = length, i.e. deleting the head.) 3. Cycle detection (Floyd) — if fast and slow meet, there is a cycle; if fast hits null, there is not.

Why it is O(1) space: you never store visited nodes, unlike a HashSet of nodes.

Source: Khamies, How to Solve Algorithm Problems, §6.1 'Detect a Linked List Cycle', §6.2 'Remove the Nth Node From the End'

fields.Recto: Merging two sorted linked lists: the invariant, and why the dummy head is mandatory here?
fields.Verso:
Keep a tail pointer on the result (starting at a dummy node). At each step append the smaller head and advance it; when one list is exhausted, append the whole remainder in O(1).

Invariant: the result so far is sorted and every remaining node is ≥ its last element.

The dummy is what lets you append before knowing which list provides the first node — without it you need a branch for the first element, which is where most bugs live. This is also the building block of merge sort (on lists) and of k-way merge (with a heap).

From your own solutions: Merge Two Sorted Lists (merge-two-sorted-lists), Merge Nodes in Between Zeros (merge-nodes-in-between-zeros)

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §4.1 'Merge of Sorted Lists'; Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.1.3, p. 33

fields.Recto: Binary tree vocabulary: height, depth, leaf, complete/full/perfect — and the convention trap?
fields.Verso:
• Depth of a node = number of edges from the root down to it (root depth 0).
  • Height of a node = number of edges on the longest path down to a leaf (leaf height 0); height of the tree = height of the root.
  • Leaf: no children. Complete: all levels full except the last, filled left to right (that is the shape a heap uses). Full: every node has 0 or 2 children. Perfect: all leaves at the same depth and all internal nodes have 2 children.

Trap: some books/LeetCode count nodes instead of edges (height of a leaf = 1). State your convention, then stay consistent — the usual source of off-by-one in tree answers.

From your own solutions: Diameter of Binary Tree (diameter-of-binary-tree), Binary Tree Postorder Traversal (binary-tree-postorder-traversal)

Source: Chatterjee, Guleria & Kiao, Binary Tree Problems, ch. 1-2 (properties, four types of binary trees) and ch. 8 'Find height or depth of a Binary Tree'

fields.Recto: The three DFS orders: what does each one give you?
fields.Verso:
• Pre-order (node, left, right): the tree as it is built — serialization, copying, prefix expressions.
  • In-order (left, node, right): sorted order for a BST; on any tree it gives the "projection" order.
  • Post-order (left, right, node): children before parent — anything that aggregates from the bottom up (heights, diameters, subtree sums, deletions), because the answer for a node needs both children's answers first.

All three are the same 5-line recursion with the visit line moved; all are O(n) time, O(h) stack (h = height).

From your own solutions: Diameter of Binary Tree (diameter-of-binary-tree), Binary Tree Postorder Traversal (binary-tree-postorder-traversal)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.2.1 'Tree Traversal', p. 41; Chatterjee, Guleria & Kiao, Binary Tree Problems, ch. 6

fields.Recto: What is the standard recursive template for tree problems, and when do you return a value vs. use a global?
fields.Verso:
Return-value style (bottom-up): solve(node) returns the information the parent needs (height, sum, is-balanced, best downward path). The parent combines left and right.

Global/closure style: the answer is not what the parent needs — e.g. the diameter goes through a node as leftHeight + rightHeight, but the parent only needs the single best height. So you return the height and update a global maximum as a side effect.

Rule: return what your parent needs; record the answer separately when it is not that. Mixing the two up is the classic tree-interview bug (returning the diameter instead of the height, which double-counts).

From your own solutions: Diameter of Binary Tree (diameter-of-binary-tree)

Source: Chatterjee, Guleria & Kiao, Binary Tree Problems, ch. 10 'Diameter of a Binary Tree' and ch. 12 'Check if a Binary Tree is Balanced by Height'

fields.Recto: Level-order traversal: why a queue, and what does the 'level size' loop buy you?
fields.Verso:
BFS on a tree = queue: pop a node, push its children. Because a FIFO pops in the order the nodes were discovered, nodes come out by increasing depth.

To process level by level, snapshot the queue length before the inner loop: for _ in range(len(q)). That freezes the current level, so the children you push belong to the next round. Nothing else gives you level boundaries for free — DFS needs an explicit depth parameter.

O(n) time, O(width) memory (which is O(n) for the last level) — the reason "does it fit in memory" matters for wide trees.

From your own solutions: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (binary-tree-level-order-traversal)

Source: Chatterjee, Guleria & Kiao, Binary Tree Problems, ch. 9 'Find Level of each node from root node'; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §6.4 'Breadth-First Search'

fields.Recto: BST invariant: what exactly must hold, and why is 'left child < node < right child' not enough?
fields.Verso:
The invariant is over whole subtrees: every key in the left subtree < node < every key in the right subtree.

Checking only the immediate children accepts invalid trees: 10 → left 5 → right 12 passes the local test (12 > 5), but 12 is in 10's left subtree and violates the order. That is why validation carries (min, max) bounds down the recursion, narrowing them at each step.

Consequences of the invariant: in-order traversal is sorted, search/insert/delete are O(h), and "k-th smallest", "validate", "range sum", "floor/ceil" are all variants of one in-order walk.

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.2.3 'Binary Search Tree', p. 46; Khamies, How to Solve Algorithm Problems, §6.4 'Validate Binary Search Tree'

fields.Recto: BST operations: complexity, and what happens in the worst case?
fields.Verso:
Search / insert / delete are O(h) where h is the height.

  • Balanced BST: h = O(log n) → O(log n) per operation.
  • Degenerate BST (sorted insertions): h = n → the tree is a linked list, O(n) per operation. This is why self-balancing variants exist (AVL, red-black).

That is the fundamental difference with a hash table: the hash gives O(1) average but no order; a BST gives ordered operations (min/max, successor, range, k-th) in O(log n) when balanced.

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.2.3-3.2.4 'BST / AVL Tree', p. 46-55; Chatterjee, Guleria & Kiao, Binary Tree Problems, ch. 33 'Binary Search Tree'

fields.Recto: Lowest Common Ancestor: how does the BST property simplify it, and what is the general binary-tree version?
fields.Verso:
BST version (O(h), O(1) space): walk from the root — if both keys are smaller, go left; if both are bigger, go right; otherwise the current node is the split point and therefore the LCA. No recursion on both sides needed.

General tree version (O(n)): post-order — if the node is null, or equals one of the targets, return it; recurse left and right; if both sides return non-null, the current node is the LCA, otherwise return the non-null side.

The two-target post-order is the pattern behind "LCA of deepest leaves" (return depth + candidate) and ancestor queries in general graphs.

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §10.2 'Lowest Common Ancestor'; Chatterjee, Guleria & Kiao, Binary Tree Problems, ch. 19 'Find ancestors of a given node'

fields.Recto: Binary heap: the two properties, the array layout, and the complexity table?
fields.Verso:
A complete binary tree (shape) that is heap-ordered (every parent ≤ its children for a min-heap). Stored in a plain array with implicit links: parent i → children 2i+1, 2i+2, parent of i → (i-1)/2.

  • peek min — O(1)
  • push (sift up) — O(log n)
  • pop (sift down) — O(log n)
  • build from an array (heapify) — O(n)

PriorityQueue in Java is a min-heap; for a max-heap use Comparator.reverseOrder(). It is a partial order — iterating it does not give sorted output, only repeated poll() does.

From your own solutions: Last Stone Weight (last-stone-weight), Minimum Amount of Time to Fill Cups (minimum-amount-of-time-to-fill-cups)

fields.Recto: Why does 'k largest elements' use a min-heap of size k, and what is the complexity?
fields.Verso:
Keep a min-heap with at most k elements. Push each value; if the size exceeds k, pop the minimum. The heap therefore always holds the k largest seen so far, and its root is the smallest of them — exactly the threshold to compare against.

O(n log k) time, O(k) memory — better than sorting (O(n log n)) when k ≪ n, and it streams (no need for the whole array).

Variants: k-th largest = the root after processing everything; "k largest in a stream" = the same structure maintained across calls (that is KthLargestElementInAStream). For the k smallest, mirror everything with a max-heap.

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.3.7 'Priority queue', p. 84; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §1.5.4

fields.Recto: Two-heaps pattern: how do you keep a running median (or a running 'lower half / upper half')?
fields.Verso:
Maintain a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balanced so that their sizes differ by at most 1. Insert into the correct half (by comparing with the other heap's root), then rebalance by moving one element.

Median = top of the bigger heap, or the average of both tops. Insert is O(log n), median O(1).

Same shape answers "find the median of a data stream", "sliding window median" (with lazy deletion), and scheduling problems where you must repeatedly take the largest below a threshold.

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.2.2 'Heap', p. 44; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §1.5.4 'Priority Queues and Heaps'

fields.Recto: Trie: node structure, the three operations and their cost?
fields.Verso:
Each node = a map/array of children + an isEnd flag. The path from the root spells the prefix.

  • insert(word) — walk/create one node per character, mark the last as end: O(L).
  • search(word) — walk the characters; must end on a node with isEnd: O(L).
  • startsWith(prefix) — the same walk without the isEnd check: O(L).

L is the word length, independent of the number of stored words. That is the property hash sets do not have: hashing destroys the prefix structure, so "is there any word starting with pre" is O(n·L) with a set and O(L) with a trie.

From your own solutions: Replace Words (replace-words), Find the Length of the Longest Common Prefix (find-the-length-of-the-longest-common-prefix)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.2.7 'Trie', p. 72; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §2.3 'Spell Checking with a Lexicographic Tree'

fields.Recto: How does a trie answer 'longest common prefix' and 'replace words by their shortest root'?
fields.Verso:
• Longest common prefix of many words: walk down from the root as long as there is exactly one child and no word ends; the path so far is the LCP. (Alternative: sort the words and compare the first and last — O(n log n) without a trie.)
  • Replace by shortest root: build a trie of the roots; for each word walk until you hit isEnd and replace by that prefix — if you fall off the trie, keep the word unchanged.

Both exploit the same thing: the trie's shared prefixes are materialised as shared nodes, so comparisons cost the prefix length rather than the word length.

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.2.7, p. 72-74 (Trie class, insert word)

fields.Recto: Adjacency list vs adjacency matrix: the trade-off?
fields.Verso:
• Adjacency list: List<List<Integer>>, one list of neighbours per vertex. Space O(V+E), iterate a vertex's neighbours in O(deg). Default choice for sparse graphs (almost all interview problems).
  • Adjacency matrix: boolean[V][V]. Space O(V²), but hasEdge(u,v) and edge updates are O(1), and it is natural for dense graphs or when the graph is given as a grid.

Grids are a special case: you do not build anything — grid[r][c] is the adjacency list, neighbours are (r±1,c), (r,c±1) with bounds checks.

Rule: E ≪ V² → list; E ≈ V² → matrix; grid → implicit.

From your own solutions: Find Center of Star Graph (find-center-of-star-graph), Find the Town Judge (find-the-town-judge)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §7.1 'Graph Representation', p. 153-155; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §6.1 'Encoding in Python'

fields.Recto: DFS: mechanism, complexity, and what it is for vs BFS?
fields.Verso:
DFS goes as deep as possible before backtracking — implemented with recursion (implicit stack) or an explicit stack. Mark a node visited when you first reach it and stop at visited nodes.

Complexity: O(V+E) with an adjacency list (every vertex and edge is examined once).

Use DFS for: connectivity/components, cycle detection, topological order (post-order reversed), "does a path exist", exhaustive exploration of states, and anything where you need the shape of the graph rather than distances. It does not give shortest paths in general — the first path it finds can be arbitrarily long.

From your own solutions: Flip Equivalent Binary Trees (flip-equivalent-binary-trees), Count the Number of Complete Components (count-the-number-of-complete-components)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §7.2.1 'DFS', p. 156; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §6.3 'Depth-First Search'; Khamies, How to Solve Algorithm Problems, §5.3 'DFS'

fields.Recto: BFS: why does it give shortest paths when all edges cost the same?
fields.Verso:
BFS explores by layers: it visits all nodes at distance d before any node at distance d+1 (a FIFO queue guarantees this). Therefore the first time a node is reached, it is reached by a shortest path — in number of edges.

Complexity O(V+E); memory O(V) for the queue, which for a wide graph can be much bigger than DFS's stack.

This is the default algorithm for "minimum number of moves/steps", "shortest path in a maze/grid", "minimum time to spread". With weighted edges the layer argument collapses and you need Dijkstra (priority queue) instead.

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §7.2.2 'BFS', p. 158; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §6.4 'Breadth-First Search'; Khamies, How to Solve Algorithm Problems, §5.2 'BFS'

fields.Recto: Grids are implicit graphs: what are the standard tricks (neighbours, visited, multi-source)?
fields.Verso:
• Neighbours: the 4-direction array {{0,1},{1,0},{0,-1},{-1,0}} (8 for diagonals), loop it instead of writing four ifs; bounds-check inside.
  • Visited: a boolean[][] (or mutate the grid) — marking at push time, not pop time, prevents duplicates in the queue. This is the #1 BFS bug.
  • Multi-source BFS: seed the queue with all starting cells and run one BFS → gives the distance to the nearest source in O(V+E), instead of one BFS per source.
  • Implicit state: when moves change a configuration (locks, water jugs), the "node" is the whole state and the visited set holds states, not cells.

Recognition: "grid + minimum steps + uniform cost" → BFS; "count regions/enclosed areas" → DFS flood fill.

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §6.2 'Implicit Graphs' and §3.1 'Shortest Path in a Grid'; Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §7.1.2 'Adjacency List', p. 155

fields.Recto: Counting connected components: the standard loop, and the 'visited' discipline?
fields.Verso:
``` count = 0 for v in vertices: if not visited[v]: count += 1 dfs(v) # marks the whole component ```

Every vertex and edge is touched once → O(V+E). The outer loop is what handles disconnected graphs; forgetting it is the classic "works on the example, fails on hidden tests" bug.

For dynamic connectivity (edges arrive one by one) or repeated "are u and v connected" queries, swap DFS for Union-Find — it answers each merge/query in near O(1) instead of re-running O(V+E).

From your own solutions: Count Servers that Communicate (count-servers-that-communicate), Count the Number of Complete Components (count-the-number-of-complete-components)

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §6.5 'Connected Components'; Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §7.2.1, p. 156

fields.Recto: Cycle detection: undirected vs directed — why are the algorithms different?
fields.Verso:
• Undirected: an edge back to an already-visited vertex that is not your parent closes a cycle (DFS), or Union-Find: an edge whose endpoints already share a component closes a cycle. In a grid, the same rule with the predecessor cell.
  • Directed: a back-edge to a vertex on the current recursion stack (often 3-coloured: white = unvisited, grey = in progress, black = done). Reaching a grey node = cycle; reaching a black one is fine (cross/forward edge, no cycle).

Why they differ: in an undirected graph every edge is "both ways", so the trivial edge back to your parent would look like a cycle — hence the parent exception. That exception is not enough for directed graphs, where the direction of the edge matters.

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §7.2.1 'DFS', p. 156 and §7.3.1 'Union-Find', p. 161; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §6.3

fields.Recto: Union-Find: the two operations, the tree representation, and the naive complexity?
fields.Verso:
Every element points to a parent; each tree is one set, and its root is the representative.

  • find(x): climb parent until the root (a node that is its own parent) → the set identifier.
  • union(a,b): find both; if the roots differ, attach one root under the other.
  • makeSet(x): parent[x] = x.

Naive version: find is O(depth) and the trees can degenerate into a chain → O(n) per call, and n unions become O(n²). Two optimizations fix that (next card).

From your own solutions: Count the Number of Complete Components (count-the-number-of-complete-components)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §7.3.1 'Union-Find', p. 161; cp-algorithms.com 'Disjoint Set Union'

fields.Recto: The two Union-Find optimizations and the resulting complexity?
fields.Verso:
1. Path compression in find: point every visited node directly at the root (parent[x] = find(parent[x])). Flattens the tree for free. 2. Union by size/rank: attach the smaller tree under the bigger root, so the depth stays O(log n) even without compression.

Together: O(α(n)) amortized per operation — the inverse Ackermann function, ≤ 4 for any realistic n, i.e. constant for all practical purposes. With only union-by-rank it is O(log n); with only path compression it is O(log n) amortized.

This is why the whole structure is usually 20 lines of code and never the bottleneck.

From your own solutions: Count the Number of Complete Components (count-the-number-of-complete-components)

Source: cp-algorithms.com 'Disjoint Set Union' (path compression, union by size/rank, O(α(n))); Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §7.3.1, p. 161-163

fields.Recto: When do you reach for Union-Find instead of a DFS/BFS?
fields.Verso:
When the graph is built incrementally or you only need connectivity, not structure:

  • edges arrive over time and you must answer "are these connected now" (offline DFS can't),
  • you only need to know if adding an edge creates a cycle (Kruskal, redundant connection),
  • you must count or merge components while merging sets, and re-running O(V+E) each time would be too slow,
  • the relation is transitive (equivalence): "same account", "same island", "same group after unions".

DFS/BFS is better when you need paths, distances, or the actual component members.

Typical size trick: keep a size[]/count array next to parent[] so the component size is O(1) after a find.

fields.Recto: Why is O(n log n) a wall for comparison sorting, and why does 'sort first' solve so many problems?
fields.Verso:
A comparison sort must distinguish n! possible orders, and each comparison gives 1 bit → log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. No comparison-based algorithm can beat that (counting/radix sort escape it by not comparing).

That bound is why sorting first is such a strong opening move: after sorting, equal elements are adjacent, the minimum and maximum are at the ends, and two pointers / binary search become applicable. Sorting costs O(n log n) and usually buys back more.

Signature in the statement: "any order", "pairs", "interval", "duplicates", "k-th" — sort, then scan.

From your own solutions: Array Partition (array-partition), Relative Sort Array (relative-sort-array)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, ch. 4 'Sorting Algorithms', p. 89-103; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §1.6.1

fields.Recto: Counting sort: when does it beat comparison sorting, and what does it cost?
fields.Verso:
When keys are small bounded integers (grades 0-100, characters, values 1..n): count occurrences in O(n), then write the values back in key order.

O(n + k) time and O(k) extra space, k = key range. It is stable if you iterate the input in order while filling (important when the key is only part of a record).

It is the engine behind "relative sort array", "sort colours", "frequency sort", histogram-type problems — and the reason a 26-slot frequency array + rebuild is O(n) instead of O(n log n).

fields.Recto: Java comparators: the correct idioms, and the two classic bugs?
fields.Verso:
• Integer.compare(a, b) — never a - b (it overflows for large/negative values), never (int)(x - y) on longs.
  • Comparator.comparingInt(Function), .thenComparing(...), .reversed() for multi-key ordering.
  • Arrays.sort(int[]) is dual-pivot quicksort (not stable); Arrays.sort(Object[])/List.sort is TimSort (stable). Sorting an int[] with a custom order requires boxing to Integer[].
  • Comparing Strings: compareTo, not ==.

Stability matters when you sort by one key and rely on a previous sort for ties (e.g. "sort by score, keep alphabetical order for equal scores").

fields.Recto: What makes a greedy algorithm correct, and how do you prove it?
fields.Verso:
Two ingredients: greedy-choice property (a locally optimal choice can be part of some global optimum) and optimal substructure (after the choice, the rest is the same problem on a smaller input).

The proof is an exchange argument: take an optimal solution that differs from the greedy one at the first step, and swap the greedy choice in — showing the result is still feasible and no worse. Repeat until the greedy solution is optimal.

Without such an argument you have a heuristic, not an algorithm. The discipline pays off: if the exchange fails, you usually need DP (the counterexample tells you what the DP state must remember).

fields.Recto: The classic greedy trap: 'pick the shortest interval first' — why does it fail?
fields.Verso:
For maximum non-overlapping intervals, the correct rule is earliest finishing time, not shortest, not earliest start.

  • Shortest first fails: a tiny interval in the middle can block two longer ones that do not overlap each other.
  • Earliest start first fails: one long interval starting early can swallow the whole timeline.

Why earliest-end works: the interval that finishes first leaves the largest remaining room for everything after it, so it is always safe to take (exchange argument: replace the first interval of any optimal solution by it — nothing after gets blocked).

Lesson: the greedy key must be the one the future depends on. "Sort by end" is the answer for selection problems, "sort by start" for merging problems.

Source: Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §3.1 'Examples' / 'Collecting Signatures', p. 124-126 and p. 146; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §5.3 'The Interval Point Cover Problem'

fields.Recto: 'Sort, then pair adjacent elements' — which problems is that the answer to, and why?
fields.Verso:
When the cost is a function of differences or matching, the optimal pairing is between neighbours in sorted order:

  • max sum of min(pair) (array partition) — pair adjacent, sum the smaller of each pair;
  • minimum total distance to seats (min moves to seat everyone) — sort both sides and pair in order (exchange argument: any crossing pair can be uncrossed without increasing the cost);
  • minimum absolute difference pairs, "maximum product of two elements", "largest perimeter triangle" (sort descending, take the first triple forming a triangle).

The underlying fact: for a sorted sequence, an uncrossed matching is never worse than a crossed one. That is a one-line exchange argument you can reuse everywhere.

fields.Recto: Binary search on a sorted array: the invariant that prevents infinite loops?
fields.Verso:
Maintain lo/hi as candidate bounds and shrink them, never recompute from scratch. Two equivalent styles:

1. while (lo <= hi): mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2; if found return; else hi = mid-1 or lo = mid+1. The window shrinks every iteration → terminates in O(log n). 2. while (lo < hi): mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2; hi = mid or lo = mid+1. Requires answers that are monotone (predicate), and terminates when lo == hi.

The invariant is the point: everything left of lo is ≤ target, everything right of hi is > target. Use lo + (hi-lo)/2, not (lo+hi)/2 — the latter overflows for large ints and misbehaves for negative ranges.

From your own solutions: Binary Search (binary-search), Longest Subsequence With Limited Sum (longest-subsequence-with-limited-sum)

Source: Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §6.2.1 'Binary Search', p. 181; Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §5.1 'Binary Search', p. 116

fields.Recto: Lower bound vs upper bound — and what does each one return on duplicates?
fields.Verso:
On a sorted array with duplicates:

  • Lower bound = first index where a[i] >= x (insertion point, keeps duplicates on the right).
  • Upper bound = first index where a[i] > x (insertion point after all copies).

So the count of x is upper − lower, and the range of x is [lower, upper). All are O(log n) — the trick is to keep searching after finding a match instead of returning immediately.

Building block for: first/last occurrence, "how many elements < x", "insert position", and any "first index where predicate is true".

From your own solutions: Longest Subsequence With Limited Sum (longest-subsequence-with-limited-sum)

Source: Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §6.2.2 'Binary Search with Duplicates' (first occurrence), p. 185

fields.Recto: Binary search on the answer: how do you recognise it and set it up?
fields.Verso:
When the answer is a number and you can write a monotone predicate feasible(x) ("can we do it with capacity x?"), binary search over the value range instead of the array:

``` lo, hi = min_possible, max_possible while lo < hi: mid = lo + (hi-lo)//2 if feasible(mid): hi = mid # mid works, try smaller else: lo = mid+1 # mid too small return lo ```

Requires feasible to be monotone (false…false,true…true). Cost: O(log(range) × cost of the check).

Recognition: "minimise the maximum", "maximise the minimum", "smallest capacity/speed/size such that…", "how many days/operations at least". The check itself is usually a greedy O(n) scan.

Source: Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §6.1 'Dividing the search space', p. 165-169; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §1.6.2

fields.Recto: Binary search in a rotated sorted array: how do you decide which half is sorted?
fields.Verso:
[4,5,6,7,0,1,2']: compare a[mid] with a[hi] (or a[lo]):

  • If a[mid] > a[hi], the right half is the rotated (unsorted) one → the minimum is right of mid.
  • Otherwise the left half is the sorted one and mid is a candidate minimum → search left.

For plain search/target: after computing mid, determine which side is sorted, and check whether the target falls inside that sorted range — if yes search there, otherwise search the other side.

Key point: the rotation keeps the "find the pivot" sub-problem monotone, so it is still O(log n) — one extra comparison changes the branch, not the complexity.

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §5.1 'Binary Search', p. 116-117

fields.Recto: The four classic binary-search bugs?
fields.Verso:
1. Infinite loop: lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1 when the window must shrink; always move at least one bound past mid. 2. Wrong bound update: hi = mid vs hi = mid - 1 must match the loop condition (lo <= hi vs lo < hi). Pick one style and never mix. 3. Overflow in (lo+hi)/2 → use lo + (hi-lo)/2. 4. Missing monotonicity: applying binary search to a predicate that is not monotone (unsorted data, or a check with side effects) gives a plausible-looking wrong answer.

Sanity test: a 2-element array (lo=0, hi=1) and an empty range — if those two cases are right, the loop is almost always right.

Source: Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §6.1 'Finding a White-Black Pair' / 'Finding a Peak', p. 167-170

fields.Recto: The two properties a problem needs before DP applies?
fields.Verso:
1. Optimal substructure — the optimal solution of the whole is built from optimal solutions of sub-instances (best(i) = min/max over choices of cost + best(smaller)). 2. Overlapping subproblems — the same sub-instance is reached by several paths, so caching pays. Without overlap you have plain divide-and-conquer (merge sort), with it you have DP (Fibonacci).

If the choices are only locally comparable and no overlap exists, you probably have a greedy problem instead; if there are no choices, it is a simulation.

The design step is always the same: define the state, then the transition, then the base case, then the order of evaluation.

Source: Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §7.1 'The Main Idea', p. 218-221; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §1.6.5

fields.Recto: Memoization vs tabulation: the trade-offs?
fields.Verso:
• Memoization (top-down): recursion + a cache, computed lazily. You write the recurrence literally; only reachable states are computed. Cost: O(depth) stack, and the recursion overhead.
  • Tabulation (bottom-up): fill a table in dependency order, iterative. No stack, cache-friendly, and it makes space optimization visible (if dp[i] only uses dp[i-1], keep two variables).

Both are O(states × transitions). Rule of thumb: write memoization first to get the recurrence right, then convert to tabulation if you need speed/depth, then shrink the memory.

Warning: recursion depth in Java is ~10⁴ frames — a 10⁵-deep recurrence must be tabulated.

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §2.1.1 'Memoization', p. 15; Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §4.1.1 'Solution 3: Memoization', p. 92-93 and §7.1, p. 220

fields.Recto: 'Define the state' — what does a good dp[...] definition contain, and how do you test it?
fields.Verso:
A good state definition answers: "dp[i] = the best/count of X for the prefix/instance …" — it names the sub-problem, not the implementation.

Checklist:

  • Is the state sufficient? (does it contain everything the transition needs — index, remaining capacity, last choice, parity…)
  • Is the state minimal? (dropping a component that the transition never reads shrinks the table)
  • Do the base cases fall out of the definition naturally (empty prefix, zero capacity)?
  • Is there a clear evaluation order (i increasing, capacity decreasing, both dimensions increasing)?

Test: state it in words; if you cannot, the recurrence will be wrong even if the code runs.

From your own solutions: Min Cost Climbing Stairs (min-cost-climbing-stairs), Unique Paths (unique-paths)

Source: Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §7.3 'Designing Dynamic Programming Algorithms', p. 271

fields.Recto: 1-D DP: 'take it or leave it' — the house-robber recurrence and why it is 1-D?
fields.Verso:
rob[i] = max(rob[i-1], rob[i-2] + value[i]) — either you skip house i (same as i−1) or you take it and add the best up to i−2.

The state only needs the last two answers → two variables, O(n) time and O(1) space. That collapse is the mark of a well-chosen 1-D state: only a fixed prefix of the table is ever read.

Same shape: maximum subarray (Kadane), "best time to buy/sell stock" (keep the min price so far), "climbing stairs" (counts), "decode ways" (with a validity condition on the pair).

fields.Recto: 2-D DP on a grid (unique paths): state, transition, and the space optimization?
fields.Verso:
dp[r][c] = number of ways to reach cell (r,c) = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]; first row and first column are 1 (only one way along an edge).

O(m·n) time and O(m·n) space — but each row only reads the previous row and the current row's left neighbour, so one row of size n suffices (dp[c] += dp[c-1] while scanning) → O(n) space.

With obstacles, the blocked cells have dp = 0. With a closed form, the count is the binomial C(m+n−2, m−1) — the combinatorial shortcut for the same table.

Source: Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §7.1 'Number of Paths', p. 218; Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, ch. 6 'Dynamic Programming', p. 129-131

fields.Recto: What are the two DP families on strings, and the difference that drives the recurrence?
fields.Verso:
• Subsequence DP (LCS, LIS): you may skip characters. dp[i][j] compares s[i] with t[j]; if equal, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, otherwise max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) — the two options are "skip a character of s" or "skip a character of t".
  • Alignment/editing DP (edit distance, wildcard matching): the three moves are insert / delete / replace, so the transition is a min over three neighbours (i-1,j), (i,j-1), (i-1,j-1) plus 0 or 1 cost.

Both are O(n·m) time and space (often reducible to O(min(n,m)) space). Writing down what a dp cell means in words ("LCS of the first i and first j characters") is what tells you which neighbours to look at.

From your own solutions: Regular Expression Matching (regular-expression-matching), Is Subsequence (is-subsequence)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §6.2 'LCS', p. 134 and §6.3 'Edit Distance', p. 137; Kulikov & Pevzner, Learning Algorithms Through Programming and Puzzle Solving, §7.2.3-7.2.4, p. 234-248

fields.Recto: LIS in O(n log n): what does the 'tails' array hold, and why is it not the LIS itself?
fields.Verso:
Keep tails[k] = the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each x, binary-search the first tails[k] >= x and replace it (or append if x is larger than all).

tails is sorted, hence the binary search, hence O(n log n). Its length at the end is the LIS length — but the array itself is not an LIS (a smaller tail is always better for extending, so tails get overwritten).

To rebuild the actual subsequence you must store predecessor indices. The O(n²) DP (for each i, best length ending at i) is the version you write first to understand it.

From your own solutions: Longest Square Streak in an Array (longest-square-streak-in-an-array)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §6.1 'LIS', p. 130 and §6.1.1 'LIS with Binary Search', p. 132; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §3.4 'Longest Increasing Subsequence'

fields.Recto: The bitwise operators and the identities worth memorising?
fields.Verso:
& AND, | OR, ^ XOR, ~ NOT, << >> shifts (>> on negatives is arithmetic = sign-extending; >>> is logical).

Identities:

  • x & (x-1) clears the lowest set bit; x & (x-1) == 0 ⟺ x is a power of two.
  • x & (-x) isolates the lowest set bit.
  • x >> k = ⌊x / 2^k⌋, x << k = x · 2^k (for non-negative x).
  • x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, XOR is its own inverse → swapping a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b.
  • Integer.bitCount(x) = popcount, Integer.toBinaryString(x) for inspection.

Watch out: shifts are done on 32-bit int in Java, and 1 << 31 is negative — use 1L << 31 when you need bit 31 as a positive value.

From your own solutions: Hamming Distance (hamming-distance), Add Binary (add-binary), Flipping an Image (flipping-an-image)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §2.3 'Bitwise Operations', p. 22-25 (AND, OR, XOR, two's complement)

fields.Recto: Why does XOR find the element appearing once, and what is the general parity trick?
fields.Verso:
XOR is associative and commutative, and x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x. So XOR-ing the whole array cancels every value that appears an even number of times, leaving the odd one out.

Variants:

  • one element appears once, all others twice → XOR of everything = the answer;
  • elements appearing twice → XOR of [1..n] and of the array, then XOR both = the missing number;
  • "find the XOR of numbers which appear twice" → XOR the values whose count is 2 (or XOR all and cancel the singles, depending on the statement).

If two elements appear once and the rest twice: XOR gives a^b; split the array on a set bit of a^b and XOR the two halves separately.

From your own solutions: Find the XOR of Numbers Which Appear Twice (find-the-xor-of-numbers-which-appear-twice), Count Pairs Of Similar Strings (count-pairs-of-similar-strings)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §2.3.3 'XOR operator', p. 24

fields.Recto: Two's complement: why does Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 become negative, and what is the safe habit?
fields.Verso:
Java int is 32-bit two's complement: the range is −2³¹ … 2³¹−1, and adding 1 to MAX_VALUE wraps to MIN_VALUE silently (no exception). Negation is ~x + 1, which is why -x == ~x + 1.

Consequences to internalise:

  • a + b can overflow even when both are positive → compare with a > MAX - b, or compute in long.
  • (lo + hi) / 2 overflows → lo + (hi - lo) / 2.
  • Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is still negative.
  • Binary search over sums / prefix sums / products: use long whenever the bound exceeds ~2·10⁹.

This is the #1 source of "correct algorithm, wrong answer on big tests".

From your own solutions: Add Binary (add-binary)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §2.3.4 'Two's complement', p. 25

fields.Recto: Euclid's algorithm, LCM, and the overflow trap?
fields.Verso:
gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b), base gcd(a, 0) = a — O(log min(a,b)) because the remainder at least halves every two steps.

lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b — divide first, otherwise a * b overflows for values around 10⁹ even though the lcm fits in a long.

Java has BigInteger.gcd for huge values, and Math.gcd-style helpers from java.math.BigInteger. For arrays: fold the gcd pairwise (reduce), and note gcd is associative.

Related: Bézout coefficients (ax + by = gcd), used to invert modulo m.

From your own solutions: Insert Greatest Common Divisors in Linked List (insert-greatest-common-divisors-in-linked-list)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §9.3 'Euclidean Algorithm', p. 231; Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §14.1 'GCD'

fields.Recto: Primality and the sieve: what are the standard methods and their complexity?
fields.Verso:
• Trial division: test divisors up to √n → O(√n) per query. Enough for single values up to ~10¹².
  • Sieve of Eratosthenes: mark multiples from p² for each prime p ≤ √n → O(n log log n) time, O(n) memory, gives all primes ≤ n.
  • Segmented sieve: sieve a range [L, R] using primes up to √R — for large values but small intervals.

Facts worth knowing: every composite ≤ n has a factor ≤ √n; 1 is not prime; 2 is the only even prime; n % 2 == 0 shortcuts remove half the candidates.

Sieve variants compute the smallest prime factor (SPF), enabling O(log n) factorisation per number.

From your own solutions: Prime In Diagonal (prime-in-diagonal)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §9.1 'Prime Numbers', p. 222 and §9.1.1 'Sieve of Eratosthenes', p. 223

fields.Recto: Fast exponentiation: the recurrence, and why it is O(log n)?
fields.Verso:
``` pow(a, n): if n == 0: return 1 if n is even: return pow(a, n/2)^2 else: return a * pow(a, n//2)^2 ```

The exponent halves every call → ⌈log₂ n⌉ multiplications instead of n.

With a modulus, reduce at every multiplication ((x*y) % m) and use long intermediates — int products overflow for m near 10⁹. This is the standard way to compute a^n mod m for n up to 10¹⁸, and the basis of modular inverse (via a^(m-2) when m is prime).

From your own solutions: Count Good Numbers (count-good-numbers), Power of Three (power-of-three)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §5.2 'Binary Exponentiation', p. 117

fields.Recto: Combinatorics basics: when do you add, when do you multiply, and what is C(n,k) used for?
fields.Verso:
• Sum rule: mutually exclusive choices → add. Product rule: independent successive choices → multiply.
  • Permutations (order matters): n! total, n!/(n−k)! for ordered k-subsets.
  • Combinations (order ignored): C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!) = C(n−1,k−1) + C(n−1,k) (Pascal). Compute iteratively C *= (n-i); C /= (i+1) to stay in integers.
  • Grid paths from (0,0) to (m,n) with right/down moves = C(m+n, m) — the closed form behind "unique paths".
  • Subsets count 2ⁿ, which is why "enumerate all subsets" is O(2ⁿ) and "bitmask DP" applies for n ≤ ~20.

Counting "at most/at least one" → complement: total − none.

From your own solutions: Unique Paths (unique-paths), Sum of All Subset XOR Totals (sum-of-all-subset-xor-totals)

Source: Dürr & Vie, Competitive Programming in Python, §14.3 'Binomial Coefficients'; Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, ch. 9 'Number Theory and Combinatorics', p. 221

fields.Recto: Digit arithmetic: what is the standard loop, and the traps?
fields.Verso:
To process the digits of a non-negative integer:

``` while (n > 0) { digit = n % 10; n /= 10; ... } ```

Building a number digit by digit: res = res * 10 + digit (watch overflow — reverse of 1534236469 does not fit in an int).

Traps: negatives (n = -n first, and remember the sign), n = 0 (the loop body never runs — handle it separately), and using Math.abs on MIN_VALUE. For base conversion the same loop with the new base, collecting digits into a StringBuilder and reversing at the end (or prepending, which is O(n²)).

Digit DP (counting numbers with a digit property in a range) is the same idea with state = position + tight flag.

fields.Recto: Segment tree: what problem does it solve that a prefix sum cannot?
fields.Verso:
Range query + point update, both in O(log n) — the case prefix sums cannot handle, because they answer queries in O(1) but need O(n) per update (and arrays answer updates in O(1) but queries in O(n)).

Structure: a binary tree over index ranges; each node stores the aggregate of its interval (sum, min, max, count, OR…). Build O(n), update O(log n) (only the path to the leaf), query O(log n) (combine the O(log n) canonical nodes).

It works for any associative aggregate (not just invertible ones like sum) — min/max/gcd/count are all fine. That is its advantage over a Fenwick tree.

From your own solutions: Count Subarrays With Majority Element I (count-subarrays-with-majority-element-i), Fruits Into Baskets II (fruits-into-baskets-ii)

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.2.5 'Segment Tree', p. 64; cp-algorithms.com 'Segment Tree'

fields.Recto: Fenwick tree (BIT): the idea in one sentence, and its complexity?
fields.Verso:
A Fenwick tree stores prefix sums in a forest where node i covers the last i & -i elements, so add(i, delta) walks i += i & -i upward and prefix(i) walks i -= i & -i downward — both in O(log n) with a single array of size n+1 and ~10 lines of code.

  • update point: O(log n)
  • prefix sum: O(log n)
  • range sum: two prefixes

It only supports invertible aggregates (sum, XOR, count) — no min/max, no range assignment. When that is enough it beats a segment tree on constants, memory and code size.

Source: Esparza Alba & Ruiz Leal, Algorithms for Competitive Programming, §3.2.6 'Binary Indexed Tree (BIT)', p. 68; cp-algorithms.com 'Fenwick Tree'

fields.Recto: Binary lifting: what does it compute, and why O(log n)?
fields.Verso:
Precompute up[k][v] = the 2ᵏ-th ancestor of v (up[0][v] = parent(v), up[k][v] = up[k-1][ up[k-1][v] ]). Then:

  • k-th ancestor = decompose k in binary and jump → O(log n) instead of O(k);
  • LCA(u,v) = lift the deeper one to the same depth, then lift both together from the highest power down → O(log n).

Space O(n log n), build O(n log n). It is the "doubling" trick (the same idea as binary exponentiation, applied to a functional graph or a tree) and it also powers "k-th successor in a functional graph" (functional graph cycle queries).

fields.Verso:
→ Two pointers from both ends. Move the left pointer up when the sum is too small, the right pointer down when it is too big. For 3-sum, fix one element and two-pointer the rest → O(n²).

Not sorted? Either sort first (O(n log n)) or use a hash map of complements (O(n) time, O(n) space).

fields.Verso:
→ Sliding window. Fixed size k → build the first window then slide (sum += enter - leave). Variable → expand right, while invalid: shrink left, record the answer.

fields.Verso:
→ Prefix sums + hash map of prefix frequencies. Walk j and count earlier prefixes equal to pre[j] - k (or the right residue mod k). O(n) instead of O(n²).

→ Hash set / hash map, one pass. Insert what you see; the answer is usually found the moment the lookup succeeds.

fields.Recto: Shape: top k / k-th largest / 'keep the k best' / k-way merge.
fields.Verso:
→ Heap (priority queue). k largest → min-heap of size k (pop the smallest when the size exceeds k): O(n log k), O(k) memory, works on a stream. k-way merge → min-heap of the k current heads.

Need the k-th smallest in a static array and no updates? Quickselect is O(n) average; sorting is O(n log n) and often good enough.

fields.Recto: Shape: 'next greater / next smaller element', 'how many days until a warmer temperature', 'span/discount to the right'.
fields.Verso:
→ Monotonic stack, one pass, O(n) amortized. Pop while the top violates the order; the popped element's answer is the current index. Increasing stack → next smaller; decreasing stack → next greater.

Scanning right-to-left gives 'next', left-to-right gives 'next after processing' — pick the direction that lets you answer on pop.

fields.Recto: Merging / inserting intervals: the algorithm and why sorting by start is the right key?
fields.Verso:
Sort the intervals by start, keep a current interval and sweep:

  • if next.start <= current.end → they overlap, merge: current.end = max(current.end, next.end);
  • otherwise flush current to the result and take next as the new current.

Sorting by start guarantees that once you reach an interval, everything already merged ends no later than it starts — so a single pass suffices, O(n log n) dominated by the sort.

"Insert interval" is the same sweep with the new interval merged in place: copy the intervals strictly before it, absorb everything that overlaps, then copy the rest. Do not re-sort: the input is already sorted, so the whole thing is O(n).

fields.Recto: Selecting the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals: which sort key, and what is the exchange argument?
fields.Verso:
Sort by end time ascending, then greedily take an interval if its start is ≥ the end of the last taken one.

Exchange argument: let G be the greedy pick with the earliest end, and O any optimal solution whose first interval is f. Since G.end <= f.end, swapping f for G leaves every later interval of O feasible (it only relaxes the constraint), so O' = O − {f} + {G} is still optimal and agrees with the greedy choice → by induction greedy is optimal.

Sorting by start or by length fails: one early-starting long interval, or one tiny interval in the middle, blocks more than it contributes.

Same rule for "burst balloons with arrows", "minimum lecture halls" (variant: sort starts and ends separately), and "erase overlapping intervals".

fields.Recto: Floyd's algorithm, part 2: why do the fast and slow pointers meet, and how do you find the cycle's entry?
fields.Verso:
Meeting: once both pointers are inside the cycle, the fast one gains exactly 1 position per step on the slow one, so the gap (mod cycle length) must reach 0 within one lap.

Entry point: let a = distance head → entry, b = distance entry → meeting point, c = cycle length. Slow travelled a + b; fast travelled a + b + k·c; fast = 2·slow ⟹ a + b = k·c ⟹ a ≡ −b (mod c). So a pointer restarted at head and a pointer left at the meeting point, both moving one step at a time, arrive at the entry simultaneously.

O(n) time, O(1) space — no hash set of visited nodes needed. If you only need "is there a cycle", stop at the first meeting.

Source: Khamies, How to Solve Algorithm Problems, §6.1 'Detect a Linked List Cycle'

fields.Recto: What exactly does Arrays.binarySearch return when the key is absent, and how do you turn that into an insertion point?
fields.Verso:
• Found → the index of some occurrence (not necessarily the first — duplicates are unspecified).
  • Not found → -(insertionPoint) - 1, where insertionPoint is the index of the first element greater than the key.

So insertionPoint = -(result) - 1 and the check is if (result < 0).

Traps: the array must be sorted (for the natural order of its type), the result is meaningless otherwise — no exception; on a sorted array with duplicates you still need a hand-written lower bound if you want the first occurrence; and Arrays.binarySearch on an int[] uses primitive comparisons, whereas on Integer[]/objects it uses compareTo/comparator.

fields.Recto: Isomorphic strings / word pattern: why is a one-way mapping not enough?
fields.Verso:
The mapping must be a bijection: every character of s maps to exactly one character of t and every character of t is the image of exactly one character of s.

A single map (s→t) accepts "bad" pairs: s = "ab", t = "aa" — a→a, b→a is consistent one way, but two different letters collapse onto one. You need the reverse check too, typically a second map or a HashSet of used targets.

Same shape for "word pattern" (words instead of letters) and for detecting a consistent relabelling of a sequence. Complexity O(n) with hash maps, O(1) with a 26-slot array when the alphabet is lowercase.

fields.Recto: Longest common prefix of a set of strings: the two standard solutions?
fields.Verso:
1. Vertical scan: compare character i of every string; stop at the first mismatch or the first string that ends. O(total characters) worst case, O(1) extra memory, early exit on the first divergence. 2. Sort and compare the extremes: after sorting, the LCP of the whole array equals the LCP of the first and last strings (everything in between shares that prefix because sorted order is lexicographic). O(n log n) for the sort + O(|first|) comparison — less code, but no early exit.

Choosing between them: few long strings that differ early → vertical scan wins; many short strings → sorting is simpler.

Trap: strs empty, or a string being a prefix of another (the loop must stop at min length).
